Review target: `PR 1471 ENG-2298 Obsidian import panel names a Roam space after one of its authors`

`minimal prompt → single careful diff pass → ≤15 findings`

You are reviewing a pull request for real bugs. Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

Review the diff as a careful senior engineer would: read every hunk, open the surrounding files for context as needed (Read, Grep, git log/blame/show), and hunt for correctness issues — wrong or inverted conditions, off-by-one, null/undefined dereference, missing `await`, dropped error handling, removed guards or validations, broken callers of changed functions, races. Prefer real failure modes over style; every finding needs a concrete scenario in which the code misbehaves.

When you are done, submit at most 15 findings via the ReportFindings tool, filling its fields as defined — for each: the file path and start line, a severity, and a comment that states the issue and the concrete scenario in which the code misbehaves. Quality over quantity: include everything you genuinely believe is a real issue, and nothing you don't.

After the tool call, also restate the findings in your final reply — one line each, `file:line — summary` — so they stay visible in sessions that do not render tool output.
I'll start by fetching the PR diff.

result.output: {"baseRefName":"main","body":" https://entire.io/gh/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/trails/6 ## Reviewer brief Author in space for obsidian, per-node for Roam. Note: The old code and the ticket language assume a multi-user Obsidian vault is possible, and counted authors. True in theory with sharing, but we cannot actually detect that, so our vaults are always single-author. So all author count checks are replaced by the `authorNamePlacement` utility function in `spaceAuthorDisplay.ts`, which gates on platform. I think knowing which platforms are single vs multi-users is a valid platform check. (It should eventually go in database/src/lib, because roam needs to make the same call.) We could decide to always rely on author count instead, but I think it is a really about platform. Also: I am not convinced we should have author name per node in roam, as it represents the page creator, not the node contributors. But rethinking that is clearly a different scope. ## Verification Loom and tests ## Loom video https://www.loom.com/share/860846a250064a06b4666a9f9e8b91ff ## Scope check - [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-2298 and the final diff. - Scope beyond `Done When`: None. (It noted removing the per-node author in Obsidian, but agreed it was justified.) ## Local delegated full review - [x] Ran a comprehensive review of the entire final diff in a subagent with a fresh context. Use `$dg-delegated-full-review` when no other full-review workflow is available. findings.short_summary: Multi-author Obsidian space attributed to one author
findings.summary: For an Obsidian space with more than one author, the header names an arbitrary single author and per-node names are now suppressed, so other authors' nodes are visibly misattributed.
findings.failure_scenario: A vault synced between two accounts (Obsidian Sync or git) publishes nodes with two distinct author_ids in one space. `authorNamePlacement("Obsidian")` returns "header", so ImportNodesModal.tsx:339 renders `[...authorIds][0]` — whichever author appears first in `publishedNodes` order — as the space's author, and the node-level name at ImportNodesModal.tsx:371 is gated off because placement !== "nodes". The old code showed nothing in the header and per-node names in exactly this case, so the change turns "no attribution" into "wrong attribution" with no way to tell from the panel. The PR body acknowledges multi-author vaults are possible in theory; the trade-off is deliberate but the failure mode is silent.

findings.short_summary: Platform fallthrough silently hides all author names
findings.summary: `authorNamePlacement` is not exhaustive over `Enums<"Platform">`, so a platform added to the DB enum falls through to "none" and author names disappear from the import panel with no compile error.
findings.failure_scenario: The `Platform` enum (packages/database/src/dbTypes.ts:1954) currently has only "Roam" | "Obsidian". Add a third value and regenerate dbTypes: this function still type-checks, returns "none" for the new platform, and every space from it renders with no author name in either the header or the nodes. The fallthrough also conflates "lookup failed / platform unknown" with "platform we have not decided about", so the case is indistinguishable in tests and at the call site. An exhaustive switch (or a `satisfies Record<Enums<"Platform">, …>` lookup with an explicit `undefined` branch) would make the new platform a build failure instead.

result.output: 2 findings reported.

content.text:
I read every hunk and pulled in surrounding context (the grouping loop, the `my_spaces` view definition and its nullability, `my_space_ids('partial')`, all `setGroupsWithNodes` call sites, `getUserNameById`), and typechecked the branch — clean apart from a `vitest` resolution artifact of my symlinked worktree that also hits a pre-existing test.

The refactor itself holds up. Things I specifically checked and cleared:

- **`getSpaceInfoFromIds` all-or-nothing null filter** — a row with a null `name` would now also drop the `url`, failing that space's import where the old `getSpaceUris` succeeded. But `Space.name`, `url`, `platform` are all non-null in the base table; the view only loses the nullability annotation. Defensive, not a regression.
- **`group.spacePlatform` → `nodesBySpace`** — safe only because `groupId = String(node.space_id)`, so a group is exactly one space. Worth knowing it's load-bearing.
- **Removed exports** — all four call sites (`importNodes`, `importPreview`, `templateImport`, the modal) updated; no stragglers.
- **Every `setGroupsWithNodes` updater spreads `...group`**, so `spacePlatform` survives toggles and Select/Deselect All.
- **Space-lookup failure path** — when a space is missing from `my_spaces` the import already fails on the `!spaceUri` guard, so the new "no author names" degradation is unreachable in practice.
- Query count drops from 6 round-trips to 3.

No correctness bugs. Two low-severity findings, both on the new gate:

- [spaceAuthorDisplay.ts:8](apps/obsidian/src/utils/spaceAuthorDisplay.ts:8) — a multi-author Obsidian space names an arbitrary first author in the header *and* suppresses per-node names, turning the old "no attribution" into silent wrong attribution. Deliberate per the PR body, but the failure mode is invisible.
- [spaceAuthorDisplay.ts:11](apps/obsidian/src/utils/spaceAuthorDisplay.ts:11) — not exhaustive over `Enums<"Platform">`: a third platform added to the enum type-checks and silently renders no author anywhere. An exhaustive switch or `satisfies Record<Enums<"Platform">, …>` would make it a build failure.

Both are judgment calls rather than defects — reasonable to ship as-is if you'd rather keep the gate simple.

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.
